catalog_quote: Evans (1995a:79-83) presents an analysis of Kayardild stress ... Among the former is a predominantly word initial main stress, stress on long vowels, and stress on the first syllable of compound constituents and of several suffixes. ... Stress falls on the first syllable of roots, and as in Evans' analysis, stress on suffixes is idiosyncratic: some suffixes will be analysed as underlyingly stressed, others are not. The analysis in §5.3 parts ways with that of Evans regarding the phonological basis of stress. Evans posits stress on every long vowel, but the analysis here does not (although it is certainly true that pitch peaks associated with stressed syllables are attracted to long vowels in the next syllable). Evans posit a stress on words' penultimate syllables which is subsequently removed post-lexically except if the word is breath group final. ... I do not follow that analysis. ...…
sweep_summary: Only one works with stress in the title: Goldstein 2005, an HRELP Field Trip Grant abstract (FTG0025) for an audiovisual Kayardild corpus with rhythmic/intonational annotation; read via the Internet Archive (live hrelp.org is an automated-access block-403) and. It is a documentation-project abstract, silent on stress placement; the fieldwork was Erich Round's (end-of-award report cited in Round 2010; ELAR deposit FTG0025 with 279 items) and fed Round 2009, already the catalog's deciding source. Priority low. Three sources downloaded on 09-16 were held by the project and read: Evans 1985 ANU PhD (first-hand, C.3.2: primary stress always word-initial, secondary on long vowels / penults / suffix and compound edges), Fletcher-Evans-Round 2002 and Round 2010 (intonation papers, both restate initial primary stress citing Evans 1995 and Round 2009). All confirm the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding; nothing contradicts it and nothing supersedes Round 2009. searching was done via direct download/automated download only.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Kayardild is non-contrastive. Although predictable from the form of a word and its affixes, the rules governing its placement are more complicated than in many Australian languages ... Three levels of stress may be identified: main, secondary and unstressed. ... Main stress falls on the first syllable ... Secondary stress falls on: (a) all non-initial long vowels, and non-initial short vowels whose syllable closes with a trill. (b) penultimate syllables. (c) the first syllable of the second element of a compound, of a two or more syllabled inflectional or of any derivational suffix.

new_statements.reading: Fixed word-initial primary stress on every phonological word, non-contrastive; secondary stress by weight (long vowels, trill-closed syllables), penult, and morphological edges (compound second member, polysyllabic inflectional suffixes, any derivational suffix). This is Evans's own first-hand fieldwork statement and matches the catalog's 'fixed' coding (initial main stress with idiosyncratic/morphological secondary stress) as carried by Round 2009 from Evans 1995:79-83.

tone_statements.quote: A recent study of the prosodic phonology of Kayardild [10] confirms that pitch accents are associated with stressed syllables, and boundary tones with larger prosodic domains, of which the breath group (a stretch of speech bounded by planned pauses) is the most relevant. tone_statements.quote: Secondly, with respect to the role of pitch height , there is as yet no convincing evidence that any Australian language has lexical tone or lexically contrastive pitch accent. audit.reasoning: Quote check: every piece of the deciding quotation and all four locators (pp. 323-324, 326, 329, ch.2 p. 109) are verbatim in the Round 2009 text we hold. Deciding source: a 786-pp 2009 Yale dissertation with a full stress chapter grounded in hundreds of recorded tokens and an intonation analysis; it is the best available description of Kayardild stress, and it explicitly engages the only other primary treatment (Evans 1995:79-83, itself the published form of Evans 1985 App. C.3.2). Three open sources downloaded now (Evans 1985 thesis pp. 508-509; Fletcher, Evans & Round 2002; Round 2010) all state primary/main stress on the word-initial syllable with trochaic feet, confirming the 'fixed initial, left edge' coding. tone.says: Intonation-only tone: AM analysis of Kayardild intonation in which pitch accents associate with stressed syllables (trochaic feet, initial primary stress) and boundary tones with breath groups; argues the apparently three-level plateau contours reduce to two phonological tones (H/L) plus phonologically contrastive register control. No lexical tone is posited.

sources.quote: 'earlier analyses of Kayardild [4] suggest certain syllables in words are metrically more prominent than others, in other words it has lexical stress. Primary stress is assigned to the first syllable, with complex rules for assigning secondary stress to syllables that are long, penultimate, or initiate suffixes of two or more syllables.' Intonational (ToBI-style) study; pitch accents anchor to stressed syllables.
sources.note: Restates Evans 1995 for stress: its one stress sentence (sec. 1, p. 1 col. 2) reports 'earlier analyses of Kayardild [4]', [4] = Evans, N. 1995, A Grammar of Kayardild (Berlin: Mouton): primary stress on the first syllable, secondary stress on long, penultimate or suffix-initial (2+ syllable suffix) syllables, consonants lengthened between adjacent stressed syllables. Co-authored by Evans and by Round (the record's describer), so not an independent description. Its first-hand content is intonational (ToBI-style): pitch accents (H*, L+H*) associate with stressed syllables.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the First International Conference on Speech Prosody 2002

sources.quote: Kayardild has eight remaining fluent speakers, all elderly, on Mornington and Bentinck Islands, Australia. The language is described in a grammar, a dictionary, and an initial intonational phonology, but we still lack any annotated documentation beyond a handful of texts. This project will begin building an audiovisual corpus of Kayardild ... It will produce audiovisual data with time-aligned interlinear, rhythmic and intonational annotations and translations. Prosodic transcription will be transparent for widespread use, but accompanied also by a more technical, ToBI-like key.
sources.note: Nothing about where word stress falls. It is a grant abstract for a documentation corpus (audiovisual texts with time-aligned interlinear, rhythmic and intonational annotation). The fieldwork was done by Erich Round (Goldstein was the Yale PI): Round 2010 ref [6] cites 'Round, E.R., A first Kayardild audiovisual text corpus, with prosodic annotations: End of award report (FTG0025), Yale University, 2005', and the ELAR search page for Kayardild shows the FTG0025 deposit (279 items) and IGS0039 (280 items) with Erich Round as person.
